# Shock and Recovery: Bahrain's import supply chains in 2026

*The whole project in one read. Generated by `src/summary.py` from the results of steps 4 to 6; the detailed reports
are linked at the end.*

On 28 February 2026, war in the Gulf closed the Strait of Hormuz and Bahrain's airspace. Everything that reaches
Bahrain by sea from outside the Gulf passes through that strait. This project uses Bahrain's official monthly import data to answer three
questions:

1. How far did imports fall below what they would have been without the war?
2. Which supply chains were hit hardest, and which routes broke?
3. How far had they come back, and how?

## The short answer

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| How far did imports fall? | **-54% in March**, -36% in April-May and -18% in June-July, against a forecast of imports without the war. About **BD 624 million** of everyday goods didn't arrive from Mar-Jul (-32%); likely between BD 539 and 710 million. |
| Which supply chains were hit hardest? | **Vehicles and transport** (-62%). Machinery and vehicles together were 64% of the money lost. By origin, **the Americas (-48%) and East and South-East Asia (-48%)**; goods from **GCC countries held up** (+8%). |
| Which routes broke? | **Container ships** (about a third of the usual containers from March to July), **car carriers** (none at all from April) and, in March, **planes**. |
| How did goods still get in? | **By other routes.** Containers and planes could have carried at most 46% of what arrived (by weight), so **at least 54% came over the King Fahd Causeway or by general cargo ship**. Light goods from far away held up while planes could fly: -13% in April-May (leaving out aircraft engines), against -54% for heavy goods. |
| How far had they come back? | **About two-thirds of the way** by Jun-Jul (from 46% of normal to 82%). Vehicles, clothing, East Asia and the Americas lagged. Port figures suggest supply chains kept adapting after Hormuz closed again on 11 July. |
| How do we know it's not normal ups and downs? | The forecast was **tested on 2024 and 2025 as if it were January**: nationally it missed by 5.5% a month in 2025. Its normal ranges held 88-92% of the time in testing, and every war-time gap is far outside them. |

## Words used in this summary

| Word | What it means here |
|---|---|
| **Core goods** | All imports except bulk materials (iron ore, alumina, coke and construction minerals) and precious metals (gold, silver and jewellery). These are the everyday supply chains, about three-quarters of import value. |
| **National total** (also *nationally* or *All of Bahrain*) | All core goods imports into Bahrain in a month, added together: every product from every origin, in one number. It doesn't include bulk materials or precious metals, or oil (the portal's import data covers non-oil imports only). |
| **Origin region** | Where goods came from, grouped into 9 regions by how they normally reach Bahrain. **GCC** means Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar and Oman, including the Jebel Ali and Oman free zones. |
| **Section** | One of the 21 top-level groups of the customs (HS) code, such as "Machinery and electrical" or "Vehicles and transport". Each section is made up of HS2 chapters. |
| **Series** | One line of monthly numbers: one HS2 chapter from one origin region, for example "chapter 84 (machinery) from Europe". |
| **Forecast** | What the model expected imports to be **without the war**. It was made at the end of December 2025, so it never saw any 2026 data. |
| **Miss** | How far a forecast was from what actually arrived, ignoring whether it was too high or too low, as % of actual imports. Lower is better. |
| **Normal range** | How far from the forecast a total can be in a normal year (9 times out of 10), measured in step 4's tests. Longer periods have narrower ranges. |
| **Gap** | Actual imports minus the forecast: in BD, or as % of the forecast. Negative means below normal. |
| **Real shortfall** | A gap bigger than the normal range: too big to be ordinary ups and downs. |
| **Lost imports** | The forecast minus what actually arrived, in BD. |
| **Since the war** | March 2026 to the latest month the portal has published, added together. |
| **Normal** | Two meanings, one for each kind of data. For **imports**, normal means step 5's forecast: what was expected without the war. For **port and airport figures**, which have no forecast, normal means the same months of 2025. |
| **% of normal** | Actual as a percentage of normal: 100% is normal, 50% is half. (Step 5's gap of -54% is 46% of normal.) |
| **Route** | How goods physically reach Bahrain: by container ship, car carrier or general cargo ship (all at Khalifa Bin Salman Port), by plane (Bahrain International Airport), or by truck over the King Fahd Causeway. |
| **King Fahd Causeway** | The 25 km road bridge between Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, Bahrain's only road link to the mainland. No monthly freight figures for it are published. |
| **Elimination** | Working out how much came by a route with no figures (the road) by taking away the most the other routes could have carried. |
| **Came back ...% of the way** | How much of the drop had been made up by the latest period. From 46% of normal at the worst to 82% is (82 - 46) / (100 - 46) = two-thirds of the way. Over 100% means it ended above normal. |
| **Adapting** | Finding other ways to get goods in while the usual route is shut. Used instead of "recovery" because the Strait of Hormuz closed again on 11 July and was still closed in October. |
| **BD m, kt** | Million Bahraini dinars (value) and thousand tonnes (weight). |

---

## Before you start: the idea in four steps

1. **Forecast imports without the war.** A model learns from 2021-2025 how monthly imports usually move, then, standing
   at the end of December 2025, forecasts every month of 2026 as if nothing had happened.
2. **Test the forecast on normal years first.** The same model is run on 2024 and 2025 as if it were January of each
   year. How far off it was sets a **normal range** for every total.
3. **Compare 2026 with the forecast.** A gap only counts as a **real shortfall** if it's bigger than the normal range.
4. **Look at the routes.** Port and airport figures show which routes broke. The road has no figures, so its share is
   worked out by **elimination**.

The periods used throughout:

| Period | What was happening |
|---|---|
| **Jan-Feb** | Before the war (it began on 28 February) |
| **March** | The shock: Strait of Hormuz and Bahrain's airspace closed, Mina Salman Port struck |
| **Apr-May** | Airspace reopened on 8 April, but Hormuz stayed closed and a US naval blockade began |
| **Jun-Jul** | A brief, partial reopening of Hormuz from 18 June, then closed again on 11 July |
| **Aug-Sep** | Hormuz closed again from 11 July (still closed in October) |

---

## 1. The data

* **Imports:** 1.76 million rows, one per month, 8-digit product code and origin country, from
  January 2021 to July 2026, from the Bahrain Open Data Portal.
* **Routes:** monthly figures for Khalifa Bin Salman Port (containers, ship visits, vehicles from car carriers, general
  cargo) and Bahrain International Airport (air cargo), which run two months ahead of the import data.
* **Three groups, analysed separately:** *core goods* (the everyday supply chains, about three-quarters of value);
  *bulk materials* (iron ore, alumina, coke, construction minerals: most of the weight, for a few factories); and
  *precious metals*, which follow the gold price. This summary is about core goods.
* **Cleaning:** six yearly files in three formats combined into one table; repeated shipments added together; totals
  checked month by month against the portal; port general cargo figures typed with a decimal point for a thousands
  separator repaired and marked.

---

## 2. The model: forecasting imports without the war

![Model comparison](figures/step4_2_model_comparison.png)

**What we did:** split core goods into 662 series (one HS2 chapter from one origin region) and compared four
forecasts, each tested on 2024 and 2025 as if it were January:

1. the **simple rule** (every month like last year's average month);
2. **the same month last year**;
3. a **linear model** (ridge regression) written from scratch in NumPy, solved two ways: exactly (normal equations) and
   by gradient descent, which agree to computer precision;
4. **gradient-boosted trees** (scikit-learn).

**What we found (national miss, % of actual imports):**

| Forecast | Miss in 2024 | Miss in 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear model** | 5.4% | 5.5% |
| Simple rule (last year's average month) | 6.2% | 6.2% |
| Gradient-boosted trees | 5.7% | 6.3% |

1. **The linear model won** in both years, at every level. Most of its gain comes from getting the level right while
   imports were growing.
2. **The trees never beat the linear model**, and in the 2025 final check they did no better than the simple rule
   (6.3%): with five years of noisy monthly data, their flexibility
   mostly fitted noise.
3. **The ranges work:** set on 2024 and checked on 2025, 88-92% of months fell inside
   them (the target was 90%).
4. **It got January-February 2026 right**, before the war: +3%, inside the normal range.

**Why it matters:** the whole project rests on this forecast, so it had to be tested before being trusted with 2026.

---

## 3. How far below normal were imports?

![National](figures/step5_1_national.png)

| Period | Forecast (BD m) | Actual (BD m) | Gap | Normal range | Real shortfall? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan-Feb | 784 | 806 | +3% | +/-8% | no |
| March | 385 | 178 | -54% | +/-15% | **yes** |
| Apr-May | 770 | 495 | -36% | +/-8% | **yes** |
| Jun-Jul | 788 | 645 | -18% | +/-8% | **yes** |
| **Since the war (Mar-Jul)** | 1,942 | 1,318 | -32% | +/-4% | **yes** |

* **March was the worst month.** Each period after that was better, but every war-time period was a real shortfall.
* **About BD 624 million was lost from Mar-Jul** (32% of what was expected).
* **A second model agrees:** the gradient-boosted trees put the national gap at -33%.

---

## 4. Which supply chains were hit hardest?

**The five sections that fell furthest (Mar-Jul):**

| Section | Gap | Lost (BD m) |
|---|---|---|
| Vehicles and transport | -62% | 165 |
| Footwear and headgear | -45% | 8 |
| Wood and cork | -43% | 7 |
| Machinery and electrical | -41% | 238 |
| Textiles and clothing | -41% | 26 |

**By origin (Mar-Jul):**

| Origin region | Gap | Real change? |
|---|---|---|
| The Americas | -48% | yes |
| East and South-East Asia | -48% | yes |
| Africa | -33% | yes |
| Europe | -32% | yes |
| South Asia | -32% | yes |
| Oceania | -31% | no (inside the normal range) |
| The rest of the Middle East | -16% | yes |
| GCC | +8% | no (inside the normal range) |

The pattern is about **routes**: goods made far away and shipped through Hormuz fell furthest, while goods from GCC
countries, which can come by road, held up.

---

## 5. Which routes broke, and how did goods get around them?

![Route groups](figures/step6_2_route_groups.png)

**Routes (% of the same months in 2025):**

| Route | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Aug-Sep |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Containers unloaded at the port | 33% | 32% | 30% | 47% |
| Vehicles unloaded from car carriers | 16% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| Air cargo and mail | 1% | 31% | 70% | 69% |
| Core goods arriving, by weight | 65% | 65% | 79% | - |

1. **Containers fell to about a third, and car carriers stopped.** Planes were grounded in March and came back slowly,
   never above normal.
2. **Goods with another way in held up.** Goods from GCC countries were +8% against the
   forecast; goods from beyond the Middle East -40%. In April-May,
   with the airspace open but Hormuz shut, light goods from beyond the Middle East were -13% (leaving out
   aircraft engines) against -54% for heavy goods.

![Elimination](figures/step6_3_elimination.png)

3. **At least 54% came by road or general cargo ship.** By weight, imports were at
   71% of their 2025 level while containers ran at 31%.
   Even assuming every import had come in a container in 2025, containers and planes could have carried at most
   46% of what arrived; the rest, about 660 thousand tonnes,
   must have come over the causeway or by general cargo ship. Cars made in East Asia and Europe kept arriving from May,
   with no car carrier calling.

---

## 6. How far had supply chains come back?

![Adapting](figures/step6_4_adapting.png)

* **Nationally, about two-thirds of the way** by Jun-Jul: from 46% of normal in
  March to 82%.
* **Back inside the normal range:** Europe, South Asia, the rest of the Middle East and Oceania among origins; goods from GCC countries were above normal (119%).
* **Still far below:** vehicles and transport (54%), wood and cork (64%), textiles and clothing (66%) and footwear and headgear (67%);
  Africa (55%), East and South-East Asia (61%) and the Americas (61%).
* **Part of the bounce came when Hormuz briefly reopened** (18 June to 11 July), so it isn't all adapting.
* **After July:** with Hormuz closed again, containers unloaded rose from 30% of normal in Jun-Jul
  to 47% in Aug-Sep, a sign that supply chains kept finding other ways in.

---

## What this project can't tell us

1. **The road has no figures**, so its share is a minimum worked out by elimination, not a measurement.
2. **The normal ranges come from two test years.** More normal years would make them more reliable.
3. **One kind of forecast decides the answer.** The trees give almost the same result, but both learn from the same
   five years.
4. **The port's general cargo figures needed repairs**, so conclusions don't lean on them.

## What I'd do next

1. **A "what if" range for the road's own share**, using reasonable assumptions about how much a container holds and how
   much general cargo was imports.
2. **Did products that relied on only a few supplier countries get hit harder?**
3. **Update with August onwards** when the portal publishes it, the first months with Hormuz closed and no reopening.
